items.text: Before costs, the return on the average actively managed dollar will equal the return on the average passively managed dollar.
After costs, the return on the average actively managed dollar will be less than the return on the average passively managed dollar.
These assertions depend only on the laws of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division.
A passive investor holds every security from a market in the same proportion as the market itself.
An active investor's portfolio differs from passive managers' at some or all times.
Active managers tend to trade frequently because they act on perceptions of mispricing.
The market return is a weighted average of returns on securities using beginning market values as weights.
Each passive manager obtains precisely the market return before costs.
The return on the average actively managed dollar must equal the market return because it is part of the weighted average.
Active managers pay for more research than passive managers.
Active managers incur higher trading costs than passive managers.
After costs, active management must underperform passive management due to greater expenses.
Some index funds sample the market rather than holding all securities in market proportions.
Index funds with high fees may have total costs equal to or exceeding active managers' costs.
Active managers may not fully represent the non-passive component of a market.
Empirical analyses often consider only professional or institutional active managers.
Individual investors' poor performance can make institutional active management appear better than it actually is.
Active managers sometimes hold securities outside the defined market being studied.
Equity mutual funds with cash holdings often underperform all-equity indices in up markets.
Survivorship bias excludes failed managers, inflating apparent active management performance.
Performance statistics should weight each manager's return by dollars under management at period start.
Simple averages of manager returns differ from capitalization-weighted performance averages.
Smaller money managers tend to favor smaller-capitalization stocks.
Equally weighted averages of active manager returns show bias toward smaller-capitalization stocks.
Active managers underperform in periods when small-cap stocks underperform large-cap stocks.
Some active managers can beat passive alternatives even after costs by managing minority actively managed dollars.
An investor can select active managers that collectively beat passive alternatives despite individual underperformance.
Peer group comparisons are dangerous for measuring active manager performance.
Capitalization-weighted averages of active managers underperform passive alternatives.
Managers should be compared against comparable passive benchmarks identified in advance of the measurement period.
Strong second-quarter corporate earnings are supporting U.S. equities despite AI stock turbulence.
Goldman Sachs believes recent AI weakness resembles consolidation rather than the end of the investment theme.
AI stock volatility during the past week has continued to follow the typical historical pattern following sharp Momentum rallies.
Previous extreme momentum rallies have been followed by corrections or consolidation periods.
Historical evidence and reduced investor leverage suggest an improved AI outlook going forward.
By July 31, approximately 61% of S&P 500 companies had released quarterly results.
64% of S&P 500 companies beat consensus earnings-per-share expectations by at least one standard deviation.
Excluding investment gains, S&P 500 earnings tracked approximately 26% higher year-over-year.
Including investment gains, headline S&P 500 EPS growth reached 45%.
Median S&P 500 company is delivering approximately 12% EPS growth, exceeding the 9% consensus forecast.
AI infrastructure companies account for approximately one-third of overall earnings expansion.
Technology, Media, and Telecommunications stocks showed lackluster reaction to earnings beats.
Within TMT, median companies beating expectations underperformed the S&P 500 by 192 basis points.
Non-TMT companies exceeding expectations generated median outperformance of 75 basis points.
Investors have become more demanding when evaluating highly valued technology and AI-related businesses.
Since Q3 began, bottom-up consensus estimates for 2027 S&P 500 earnings increased by 1%.
Analysts made positive revisions across most sectors in recent forecasts.
Rising input costs on margins remain a key risk identified by Goldman.
Hyperscalers recorded $182 billion capital expenditure during the quarter with only $5 billion free cash flow.
Hyperscaler debt and equity issuance reached $101 billion during the quarter.
Analysts forecast more than $1 trillion capital expenditure during 2027, a $100 billion increase from previous estimates.
Capital spending expected to exceed operating cash flow between 2026 and 2028.
Cloud revenue growth accelerated to 48% during the quarter, exceeding expectations.
Heavy AI investment is translating into stronger cloud demand based on accelerating growth rates.
Robust corporate earnings provide a buffer against continued AI stock volatility.
Research in experimental psychology suggests that, in violation of Bayes' rule, most people tend to "overreact" to unexpected and dramatic news events.
In revising their beliefs, individuals tend to overweight recent information and underweight prior (or base rate) data.

This rule-of-thumb, an instance of what Kahneman and Tversky call the representativeness heuristic, violates the principle that the extremeness of predictions must be moderated by considerations of predictability.
If stock prices systematically overshoot, then their reversal should be predictable from past return data alone, with no use of any accounting data such as earnings.
Hypothesis one: extreme movements in stock prices will be followed by subsequent price movements in the opposite direction.
Hypothesis two: the more extreme the initial price movement, the greater will be the subsequent adjustment.
Both hypotheses imply a violation of weak-form market efficiency.
Winner and loser portfolios are formed conditional upon past excess returns, rather than some firm-generated informational variable such as earnings.

The empirical analysis is based on three types of return residuals — market-adjusted excess returns, market model residuals, and Sharpe-Lintner CAPM excess returns — but only market-adjusted results are reported.
The residuals are estimated as u_jt = R_jt − R_mt; there is no risk adjustment except for movements of the market as a whole.
Monthly return data for New York Stock Exchange common stocks, as compiled by the Center for Research in Security Prices, are used for January 1926 through December 1982.
An equally weighted arithmetic average rate of return on all CRSP listed securities serves as the market index.
For every stock with at least 85 months of return data, without any missing values in between, the next 72 monthly residual returns are estimated.
At the portfolio formation date the cumulative excess returns of the prior 36 months are computed and ranked from low to high.
Firms in the top 35 stocks are assigned to the winner portfolio W; firms in the bottom 35 stocks to the loser portfolio L.
The step is repeated 16 times for all nonoverlapping three-year periods, with formation dates December 1932, December 1935, through December 1977.
If a security's return is missing in a month subsequent to portfolio formation the stock is permanently dropped, so the calculations involve an implicit rebalancing.

The requirement that 85 subsequent returns be available biases the selection towards large, established firms, countering the critique that the overreaction effect may be mostly a small-firm phenomenon.
Between 347 and 1,089 NYSE stocks participate in the various replications.
Over the last half-century, loser portfolios of 35 stocks outperform the market by, on average, 19.6% thirty-six months after portfolio formation.
Winner portfolios earn about 5.0% less than the market thirty-six months after portfolio formation.
The difference in cumulative average residual between the extreme portfolios equals 24.6%, with a t-statistic of 2.20.
The overreaction effect is asymmetric; it is much larger for losers than for winners.
In months t = 1, t = 13, and t = 25 the loser portfolio earns excess returns of, respectively, 8.1%, 5.6%, and 4.0%.
The overreaction phenomenon mostly occurs during the second and third year of the test period; twelve months in, the difference between the extreme portfolios is a mere 5.4%.
As the formation-period cumulative average residuals grow larger, so do the subsequent price reversals; for a formation period as short as one year, no reversal is observed at all.
Average betas of the winner portfolios are significantly larger than those of the loser portfolios — 1.369 versus 1.026 — so if the CAPM is correct losers are also significantly less risky.
In the five-year formation experiment with 46 yearly replications, the loser portfolio's large January returns are observed as late as five Januaries after portfolio formation.
Persistently, losers earn exceptionally large January returns while winners do not, yet the companies in the extreme portfolios do not systematically differ with respect to market capitalization.
Thirty-six months after portfolio formation the losing stocks have earned about 25% more than the winners, even though the latter are significantly more risky.
